text:
There is no meaningful token overhead of using Matryoshka. MCP tool definitions do have a fixed token cost in the system prompt, but it's amortized across the session. The savings come from per-query efficiency, not zero overhead. For a single small file, the tool definitions might exceed the savings. For repeated queries on large files, the savings compound.

Think of it as a db that Claude can run queries against. The reduction comes from the fact that Claude isn't looking at the documents directly, or even results a lot of the time. What happens is that Claude tells the MCP to load a file, and then runs queries against it, and results are bound to variables. Now Claude just needs to know about a pointer to the data instead of seeing the data and roundtripping it constantly.

Claude can also expand handles when needed (lattice_expand $res1 limit=10), but only does so when actually required for decision-making. It's not blind, but rather has on-demand visibility.

The key advantage here is in having persistent session state in the REPL. Say Claude does a search and finds all the failures, and then sum them up. With this approach Claude doesn't even need to see the actual lines themselves.

Subagents still read files into their context and do full text processing. Lattice keeps data server-side in SQLite, even the subagent equivalent would need to materialize results to reason about them.

With a subagent you're doing File → Agent context → Process → Return summary. With Lattice you do File → SQLite → Query → Handle stub → Expand only what's needed.

Finally, the synthesis/regex features are orthogonal to the token savings from handle-based queries. That's just the internal rules engine Matryoshka implements.

text:
I've been using wiki software for my own "second brain" for at least a decade now, probably more. I have written hundreds (maybe thousands) of pages at this point. I cannot recommend it highly enough: If you are a knowledge worker, you cannot possibly hold everything in memory. Those who claim they can, are fooling themselves. (The greatest engineers/scientists/researchers throughout the centuries were also incredibly habitual writers and note-takers, and I don't think this is a coincidence.)

Plus, the act of writing something down makes it more likely than not you will remember it (or at least, remember it better). At a certain point, having it available for later reference is almost more of a side-benefit.

I eventually just wrote my own knowledge base for the improved UX/ergonomics. (I'm a big fan of search over metadata curation.) Yes but no , many of these issues are and were caused by political movements and think tanks outside technology


Let’s unpack the paragraph you’re quoting.



Generative AI tools [are] powered by data centers which consume vast amounts of water and pollute our environment



Such resource consumption and pollution is kind of a requirement for AI to exist at all. You want more models, more users? You gotta have more data centres, consume more resources, and pollute quite a bit more. Speaking of which, infrasound seems to be a significant health issue for many people leaving near data centres.



Generative AI tools […], are built on the collective theft of the works of millions of artists, developers, authors, and other creatives



Again, this data collection is necessary to get good models. The only alternative would be to pay all the authors, which would likely cost more in paperwork than in copyright fees themselves. In fact, I suspect doing this correctly and ethically is likely to instantly invalidate the entire business model.

To nuance that a bit I do have issue with the term "theft" here: copyright is state granted monopoly, not actual property. Still, to the extent we accept copyright law is a good thing, there’s something wrong with the data collection necessary to teach an AI. Even if you reduced the scope of copyright to commercial exploitation and 5 years after publication, scrapping a recent news article so ChatGPT can be better at predicting the next word is a copyright violation. It’s not obvious if you frame it as "learning" and "generating" or "predicting", but I believe it’s more accurate to see models as a form of lossy compression.



Generative AI tools […], have repeatedly provoked psychosis and suicide



Significant effort needs to be spent on safety to avoid things like that, and that effort diverts resources the company could instead devote to promotion or making the model even more powerful. In fact, this is not specific to AI at all, this is just the usual tension between profitability (or competitiveness), and externalised risks so typical of our economy. Not sure we can really fix that one, short of addressing Capitalism itself. A highly political issue for sure, but one born out of the status quo, not any particular political movement.



Generative AI tools […] supercharge the spread of disinformation and fascism,



Disinformation in general, well… they do so in two ways: hallucinations, and helping people spread believable lies. The first problem is mostly technical. The second problem is more about giving people powerful tools. As for fascism… given than authoritarians are more likely to value hierarchies and in-group thinking instead of truth, I’m not surprised generative AI favours the far right more than it favours the far left here. Structurally I mean, not because any interest or political movement leaned in particularly heavily.

And do not forget the other side of the equation: recommendation algorithms and filters. There’s a reason it’s hard to widely publish, say, porn of people way too young to be legal: the biggest platforms have filters in place so they do not recommend those things, or even host them at all. The same could be said for political discourse. See what happened to the Overton window on Twitter after Musk took over. I believe this side is much more responsible for misinformation and fascism than generative AI is.

I do have to concede however that Grok is a case of a very rich, very political, not-that-technical dude causing the harm. Clearly, Grok wouldn’t so easily spout Nazi nonsense without someone like Musk in charge. Still, Grok wouldn’t be so harmful if Twitter wasn’t such an enabler.



Generative AI tools […] concentrate wealth in fewer hands while providing cover for widespread layoffs.



Again, a very general point about infrastructure being captured by, and profiting, rich capitalists instead of everyone else. Again, status quo, not any particular movement. And the solution is the same: public investments, tax the rich, regulate…

One way to look at this is to say that most of these issues were present since Capitalism is a thing, and AI, just like looms, is just one of many technologies that was captured by the system to concentrate wealth, at the expense of pretty much everything else. Then yes, this is all about political movements and think tanks outside of tech, and solving the root of the problems gets us way out of scope for this forum.

On the other hand, generative AI does uniquely amplify those problems, so avoid using it, and telling everyone we should stop using it, may very well be the only ethical way forward, given the society we’re currently living in. Wait, no, there’s also blowing up those data centres, but I’d rather not encourage crimes in any legislation where it is illegal to do so.

text:
The title of the linked-to blog post is true, and the contents are true, they just have no explicit, cause-and-effect relationship.  The title has been the desire of the management class for at least 30 years that I'm aware of. Microsoft promised managers that software engineering would pretty much go by the wayside with the introduction of Windows NT circa 1994. There was next to nothing about this in the official, printed, bumpf that went with NT, but in person, Microsoft salespeople promised managers huge programmer productivity gains, 5x-10x, and NT would make all programmers plug-compatible. Managers could just hire and fire downtrodden Windows code monkeys. This turned out to be marketing gibberish, and Microsoft lies, but back then, managers believed it.

In 1998, I worked for US WEST, one of the "Baby Bells". The Communication Workers of America struck, so suddenly, I was in management, and had to Loop Assignment. As soon as the strike was over, I wasn't in management and I had to give back my corporate AmEx card. The manager class is really uneasy about sharing power with a new group, they already have to deal with lawyers, and they hate that. The last 30 years of having to listen to software engineers as a category, and take them seriously, has been traumatic. The title of this article describes the end result of many, many attempts to stuff the genie of a new non-worker category of employees back in the lamp.

You don't have to believe me on any of this, but that doesn't make it less true.

text:
Sorry, I did an inadequate proofreading of that.

The USA had a giant telephone system, The Bell System, which served the majority of the nation until 1983. The US courts deemed it a monopoly, and caused it to be broken up into regional companies, the "Baby Bells". US WEST was one of those regional, serving as I recall 14 US states from Iowa and Minnesota, to Oregon and Washingtion. Huge land area, relatively sparse population. It's been merged and re-merged, and telephones are mostly of no use.

The Communication Workers of America was one of two unions that a lot of the non-management US WEST employees belonged to. They went on strike summer of 1998. I was not a unionized employee so by default, I was management, so I did not get to go on strike. Due to what I worked on, I knew something of the intricacies of how telephone lines were laid out, so the strike planners put me in "loop assignment".  Phone companies called the circuit from central office to customer a "local loop". We had access to the outside plant inventory, so technicians hooking up or repairing phone service had someplace to get extra help if the physical reality didn't match what their work orders said to do. Loop assignment involved looking up the work order, figuring out which pair of wires (26-gauge twisted pair, denoted by color, brown/brown-and-white for instance) could be used at a given telephone pole, or pylon or cross box, and how they should be jumpered together.

I think it will turn out fine. Digital software enabled >10-1000x the developers vs punch-cards per expensive machine. FORTRAN/COBOL/BASIC/C/Java enabled another >10-1000x growth in programmers vs the assembly population. JavaScript and the rise of the Internet and web browser + SaaS enabled another 10-1000x more programs than we were capable of deploying before, as a species.

For proof, see my PS5 unable to play Fortnite because the devs released yet another 100GB update. Pay no mind to how much RAM we went to the moon with, and how no "engineer" we think of when reading these articles has read NASA's coding guide from then. Look instead forward: the update's contents could have been streamed to me as needed, while I was playing, saving Epic cloud costs and giving me another evening in which to buy skins. Why haven't they built it?

Yes, right now AI turns out horribly wasteful and bad results. Every leap forward in abstraction has, when used by the clueless/useless. But the bottleneck is still the human mind, still the interface from the computer to the real world, still the same as it always was.

Pushing programming forward has often been about being the most hard-headed and motivated to build something that you believed possible. The bar just lowered a bit on the two-decade/computing-era scale of things, but it will still take a lifetime for the majority of the working population to catch on and be presented with the advantage, by which time the leading edge will have moved. The majority of the programming population...well...we've always had to keep up.

It will turn out the same way it always has. With lots of awesome advancements, and some disasters along the way thanks to man's hubris, see Therac-25's software cost-savings strategy. As individual engineers who don't take on further responsibility, we can only control our own contributions to each category. And man, I have seen some really cool things built and used daily by guys who would in the past never dreamed of even talking to a programmer, in some cases even using software instead of paper!

Personally, in the long term, I worry about how things turn out if articles like this are the reading material of today's up and coming. For everyone else there's influence: firing, stern talking to, removing merge rights, admitting that you're not the most senior, venting online, or confronting your own role in your own life.

I know which I would have chosen before I had a year to meditate on it.

text:
One thing noted here is "rigor". I'm beginning to come to the conclusion that rigor as we know it will die with LLMs.

We (as in software engineers) can't keep talking about long-running agents, sub-agent fleets, agents changing themselves and writing tools for themselves at runtime etc etc and fool ourselves that this can all happen with any sort of upfront rigor check during CI with testing and such. The dynamic and non-deterministic outcomes prevent this.

I think we need to start running with the idea that we will be essentially yolo'ing things without humans in the loop to prod, and what that means for "rigor" . For me, I'm thinking what we are looking at is moving a lot of software verification to long running sandboxes and canaries. Is the agent doing what was asked? Are objectives being met? Are invariants being violated? Then we send it on to prod, and start acting with extreme prejudice against the process: as soon as it looks like it's going wrong, the process is aborted and started again.
